catalog_quote: [Artuso 1998 §2.4.3] In Anishinaabemowin, syllables that occur word finally or have long vowels are always strong. Short vowels may fall in either strong or weak syllables, often being deleted in the latter case in a similar manner to the Odaawaa dialect (Rhodes and Todd 1981:58). Anishinaabemowin syllables make up iambic feet, i.e. weak-strong. If the first syllable in a word contains a short vowel, this vowel will be weak and then the second syllable will be strong, after which we will find another weak syllable, unless there is a long vowel in this position. If the first syllable of a word contains a long vowel, this syllable will be in a foot of its own and the second syllable will be weak, etc. ... Note that since final syllables are always strong, these are never deleted due to stress. The addition of personal prefixes may cause alternations in the stress pattern of a stem, see 3.…

audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations verified verbatim in copies we hold at the stated locators (Artuso 1998 §2.4.3 = PDF p.24; Redish & Lewis 'Algonquin Stress'). (2) The classification 'weight-hedged' (quantity-sensitive iambic, long vowels always strong, L-to-R, final syllable strong) rests on a 1998 MA thesis sketch; I downloaded the two professional phonological treatments that bear on Algonquin — Piggott 1978 (Maniwaki: stress on all tense vowels + alternating stress on even-numbered lax vowels L-to-R; initial lax vowels never deleted; 'stress placement.. not fully determined for the Algonquin dialects') and Valentine 1996 (quantity-sensitive iambic feet from the left edge for the whole Ojibwe complex incl. Algonquin; Maniwaki plural realized as final high pitch; 'stress system of northern dialects remains to be worked out') — and both confirm the weight-sensitive iambic coding. Aubin 1979/1981, Daviault et al. 1978 and Cuoq

sources.quote: For the Ojibwe complex (explicitly incl. sources.citation: Nicolas, Louis (1674). Grammaire algonquine ou des sauvages de l'Amerique septentrionelle : avec la description du pays.. N.A.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: The catalog record for Algonquin has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements; this 1674 source adds nothing on stress placement. Its 'accens' passage is a length contrast, so it should not be read as evidence of lexical or unpredictable stress. Nicolas's language is 17th-century Old Algonquin of the Ottawa River / Nipissing region (he refers to 'les Outaouaks' in the pronunciation remarks), the ancestor of modern Algonquin rather than any present-day community's speech.
